---
title: "Opening: A Diagnostic Moment"
---

::: {.callout-schedule icon=false}
## Duration: 10 minutes
:::

## Welcome

Before we get into theory, a moment of recall.

## Think-Pair-Share: a misdiagnosis you remember

::: {.callout-individual icon=false}
## THINK (3 minutes)

Bring to mind a moment when you misjudged what a student knew or what was going wrong with their thinking. The moment can be from any context: a written assignment, a discussion comment, an exam answer, a question they asked, a comment they made in passing.

Hold the moment for a beat. Try to recall:

- What did the student say or write?
- What did you initially conclude they did or didn't understand?
- What turned out to be actually happening?

If two moments come to mind, pick the one that was most surprising in retrospect.
:::

::: {.callout-pair icon=false}
## PAIR (4 minutes)

Tell your neighbour about your moment, and listen to theirs. Then compare:

- Were the two moments structurally similar (same kind of mismatch between your initial reading and what was actually happening) or very different?
- When you were teaching that student, did you have a clear name or category for what turned out to be going on?
:::

::: {.callout-group icon=false}
## SHARE (3 minutes)

A few volunteers share moments. The instructor will note the kinds of mismatches that come up: students with confident-sounding wrong models, students retrieving correct facts without engaging, students stuck on irrelevant features, students missing prerequisites, students juggling too many pieces.

These are exactly the categories we will use today.
:::

## The bridge to today's workshop

The diagnostic problem you just remembered is the daily work of teaching: looking at a student artifact and reading what is actually happening in their working memory.

Today's tool gives an LLM a fixed cognitive-load-theory taxonomy and asks you to teach it how that taxonomy looks in your discipline. The output is a quick, structured read on a student response: what kind of cognitive signal is it, and what intervention fits.

::: {.callout-pro-tip icon=false}
## The workshop as worked example

This workshop is itself a worked example of CLT-grounded design. The diagnostic categories are fixed by us; your work is in the discipline-specific cues. That decomposition (theory provides structure, practitioner provides domain) is the move we want you to take back to your teaching.
:::
